rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six peaks while limiting the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The retention window and critical resolutions will guide subsequent slope and temperature adjustments.
The first method reached the maximum CRF with ample resolution margin. Shorten the gradient while holding temperature and endpoints fixed to seek a faster fully resolved separation.
The 6-minute gradient retained the maximum CRF and a minimum resolution of 2.54. Reduce tG one grid step to test a faster separation while keeping the other variables fixed.

Test the shortest allowed gradient to establish the speed limit at these endpoints and temperature. The first pair may fall below 1.5; if so, the 4-minute gradient remains a fully resolved maximum-CRF method.

Return to the shortest fully resolved gradient and raise temperature to test whether elution can be accelerated without losing the first pair's resolution. This also measures temperature selectivity before further speed optimization.

Higher temperature worsened the critical pair, so test the lowest temperature with a gentler 2-minute gradient. Lowering phi1 to 0.80 may recover full resolution while allowing a shorter separation than the established 4-minute method.

Increase the final organic fraction one grid step to accelerate the late peak. The critical first pair has only a small resolution margin, so this tests whether the faster method can retain the maximum CRF.

Raise phi0 one step to reduce the gradient slope while retaining the stronger final solvent that accelerated the last peak. This tests whether the first pair can regain R ≥ 1.5 without sacrificing the shorter elution window.

Shift both endpoints upward by 0.10, preserving the slope of the successful injection 8 while strengthening the final hold. This should accelerate the last peak and tests whether the earlier pair retains sufficient resolution at higher starting organic fraction.

Increase starting organic by one grid step to shorten retention further while keeping the fastest gradient and strongest final solvent. Monitor the first pair for loss of retention and resolution as it approaches the solvent front.
Raise phi0 another grid step to seek a shorter fully resolved separation. Although the first pair improved at phi0 0.30, its proximity to the dead time makes early-peak compression the main risk.

Back off to phi0 0.30, which preserved full resolution, and raise temperature one step to accelerate the last peak. This tests whether the first pair's resolution margin can accommodate modest heating.
Increase temperature one more grid step to locate the speed–resolution boundary. The first pair may drop below 1.5; injection 12 remains the fastest tested method with maximum CRF.

Return to 30 C and lower phi1 one step to increase the critical pair's resolution margin through a gentler gradient. Since the maximum CRF is already achieved, this tests a potentially more robust, still rapid alternative to injection 12.

Lower phi0 one step to move the early peaks away from the solvent front while retaining a rapid separation. This tests whether a less aggressive starting composition can preserve maximum CRF; injection 12 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested.

Lower temperature to improve the critical first pair while retaining the short gradient. This tests a rapid alternative with more resolution margin; injection 12 already achieves the maximum CRF and remains the fastest fully resolved method tested.

Lower phi1 one further step to test whether the critical pair gains useful resolution margin while all peaks still elute rapidly. The maximum CRF is already secured; injection 12 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested.

Combine the gentler gradient with a lower starting organic fraction to keep early peaks farther from the solvent front, using modest heating to accelerate the last peak. This tests a nearby maximum-CRF alternative; injection 12 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested.

Test a lower starting organic fraction with the strongest final solvent to delay the early peaks while maintaining rapid late-peak elution. This probes whether maximum CRF can be retained with less solvent-front proximity than injection 12.

Test a gentler gradient at low temperature to increase the first pair's resolution margin while keeping it farther from the solvent front than at phi0 0.30. This refines a rapid maximum-CRF alternative; injection 12 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested.

Increase phi1 from injection 15 to accelerate the last peak while keeping the early peaks farther from the solvent front than in injection 12. This tests the remaining nearby fast-method candidate, although the first pair may lose its small resolution margin.

Lower temperature from injection 18 to improve the critical pair's resolution margin while keeping the early peaks clear of the solvent front. This explores a rapid, better-separated alternative; injection 12 remains the fastest tested method achieving the maximum CRF.

Raise temperature one step from injection 17 to shorten late-peak retention while testing whether its resolution margin is preserved. Injection 12 remains the fastest tested fully resolved method, with the maximum CRF already secured.

Lower phi1 one step from injection 19 to improve its marginal first-pair resolution while keeping the early peaks farther from the solvent front. This tests another rapid maximum-CRF option; injection 12 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested.

Lower phi1 one step from injection 24 to test a larger first-pair resolution margin with early peaks well beyond the dead time. The maximum CRF is already secured, and injection 12 remains the fastest tested fully resolved method.
